description: We are Phantom Troupe, a team of six from Rangpur, Bangladesh, working on "Dancing with the SARs". We build TeestaWatch, which uses NASA radar and our own deep-learning models to map Teesta river floods, forecast riverbank erosion, and show families when the river may reach their homes. Our skills: machine learning, remote sensing, web development, research and video. Our team is full (6 members), so we are not recruiting.
summary: We developed TeestaWatch, a free, live website that shows families along the Teesta river in northern Bangladesh where floods have reached, where the riverbank is eroding, and when the river may reach their village. Every monsoon the Teesta destroys homes and farmland, but clouds block optical satellites exactly when floods happen, and the national erosion forecast does not cover this river. For the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge, we used Sentinel-1 radar (from NASA ASF), which sees through clouds. Our own deep-learning model, TG-FloodNet, maps flood water from radar; on our 2025 test areas it scored F1 0.84, against 0.60 for NASA's OPERA DSWx-S1. A second AI forecasts next year's erosion from ten years of NASA HLS images, and our Time-to-River model gives each of 7,664 settlements (395,693 homes) its chance of being reached within 1, 3 and 5 years, tested on real past years (AUC 0.85). This matters because families get no warning today. TeestaWatch is a working prototype: it is not updated automatically yet, and Bangla SMS alerts are our next step. We wrote and tested it ourselves, using AI tools to help with code.
details:
TeestaWatch answers the question families on the Teesta river ask every monsoon: will the river reach my home, and when?

THE PROBLEM

The Teesta in northern Bangladesh floods farmland and eats its banks every year. In Lalmonirhat district alone, erosion left 12,500 families homeless in ten years (The Daily Star). The worst damage happens under monsoon clouds, when normal satellites cannot see the ground, and the national erosion forecast covers the Jamuna, Ganges and Padma, but not the Teesta. Families get no warning; help arrives after the land is gone.

WHAT IT DOES

TeestaWatch is a free, live website covering 1,609 km² of the Teesta, built from 756 satellite images (2016-2026):

- Floods: maps of four floods (2017, 2020, 2024, 2025). July 2020 alone added 475 km² of new flood water.

- Riverbank: ten years of river maps. The river took 10,777 ha of land since 2016.

- Erosion forecast: land at risk next year (281 ha high, 357 ha medium risk).

- Villages: 7,664 settlements and 395,693 homes, each with its chance of being reached within 1, 3 and 5 years. Anyone can search a village, union or upazila. Example: Lakkhitari 1 (480 homes) is 30 m from the river, with a 42% chance of being reached within 5 years.

HOW IT WORKS (SAR AT THE CORE)

1. Sentinel-1 radar sees through clouds, day and night. We order terrain-corrected (RTC) scenes through NASA ASF HyP3.

2. TG-FloodNet, our own deep-learning model, is pretrained on Sen1Floods11 and fine-tuned on the Teesta with clear-sky water labels from NASA HLS and OPERA DSWx-HLS, so it can map water from radar on cloudy days. NASADEM height helps remove false water on high land.

3. Yearly dry-season maps from NASA HLS give the riverbank history.

4. A ConvGRU U-Net learns from ten years of maps to forecast next year's erosion.

5. Our Time-to-River model (a first-passage probability model) turns each bank's past movement into the chance of reaching each building (Google Open Buildings).

HOW WE KNOW IT WORKS

- Floods: on 50 Teesta areas we labelled by hand, F1 0.82. On the 2025 test areas, F1 0.84 vs 0.60 for NASA's OPERA DSWx-S1 on the same areas.

- Erosion: tested on years it never saw (2025, 2026): AUC 0.92 and 0.95, 19x and 32x better than chance.

- Villages: using data only up to 2019, it predicted where the river reached by 2025 with AUC 0.85.

WHY IT IS CREATIVE

Most flood tools answer "where is the water now?". TeestaWatch also answers "when will the river reach this home?", turning ten years of satellite history into a chance for every building. We built our own flood model for one river and openly compared it with NASA's product.

IMPACT AND WHO IT HELPS

About 2,511 homes have a better-than-even chance of meeting the river within 5 years. Union Parishad chairmen can see who to move first, NGOs can see which char (river island) needs help, the Water Development Board can see where to protect next, and families can check their own village. Acting even one season earlier can save a harvest, seed stock or a home.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Monsoon clouds (so radar first), non-expert users (plain words, simple colours, real village names, works on phones), slow rural internet (light map files), honesty (every number is tested and explained on the How it works page), and cost (free, open data and free hosting, so anyone can repeat it).

TOOLS

Python, PyTorch, segmentation-models-pytorch, earthaccess, asf_search, hyp3_sdk, rasterio, xarray, GeoPandas, scikit-learn, QGIS, Kaggle GPUs. Website: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS, GitHub Pages. Open-source code (MIT License): https://github.com/AayatHossain/teestawatch-web

LIMITS (HONEST)

TeestaWatch is a working prototype. Maps are not yet updated automatically after each satellite pass, and it does not send alerts yet. Building outlines come from Google Open Buildings, so some homes may be missing. Risk numbers are chances, not certainties.

NEXT STEPS

Automatic updates with every radar pass, NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar, alerts in Bangla for every family, and a pilot with one partner such as the Water Development Board. Then the Jamuna, Padma and Brahmaputra: the method works on any river.

Source code (GitHub): https://github.com/AayatHossain/teestawatch-web
